units.text: Will We All Become Psychotic?

The question is powerful. Available evidence does not justify answering “yes.” Nor does it offer a simple individual probability we can apply to anyone who uses an LLM. The existence of severe cases, the existence of plausible mechanisms, and the estimation of a population risk are three different things.

A headline about someone who lost contact with reality can demonstrate that an event deserves investigation. It does not tell us how many exposed people remained well, how many would have had symptoms without a chatbot, what vulnerabilities existed, or how the risk changed over time.
The 185 Accounts

On September 7, 2026, Morrin and colleagues published a preprint based on 185 self-selected accounts received online: 95 firsthand and 90 from other people. Raters coded descriptions consistent with delusional beliefs in 102 accounts; chatbot validation appeared in 50 of those. The accounts were not confirmed through independent diagnostic assessments. The sample was oriented toward negative experiences, the analysis was retrospective, and inter-rater agreement on the presence of delusions was only moderate. The study signals possible patterns of harm; it does not show that 55% of chatbot users develop delusions and does not permit causal inferences. [14]

This is an example of a decisive denominator. A collection of people reporting problems is not a random cross-section of all users. If we calculated the breakdown risk for all cars only from vehicles that reached a repair shop, we would obtain a severely distorted picture.

The statistical analogy does not minimize the cases. A repair shop can discover a real manufacturing defect. But to learn how widespread the defect is, we also need to know what happens beyond the shop door.
Another Denominator, the Same Caution

In October 2025, OpenAI reported an estimate of approximately 0.07% of users active in a particular week whose conversations indicated possible signs of a mental health emergency related to psychosis or mania. This is a provider estimate about conversational indicators, not the percentage diagnosed, not the incidence of cases caused by the chatbot, and not a cumulative probability of developing psychosis. It cannot be directly compared with percentages in a self-selected sample of negative accounts. [45]

Small numbers do not rule out individual severity. Large numbers in a selected sample do not demonstrate universality. A mature discussion can preserve both propositions without feeling compelled to choose between advertising and panic.
A New Name Does Not Create a New Illness

The expression “AI psychosis” circulates as an informal label. In an August 2026 preprint, Au Yeung and colleagues discuss whether a distinct clinical entity would be justified. Yet the existence of a debate does not mean a new diagnostic category is already established. Defining the phenomenon, longitudinal follow-up, and distinguishing triggering from exacerbation of vulnerabilities are necessary. [15]

A technology can be the object of a delusional belief, supply material for it, or interactively participate in amplification. These roles are not identical. If people in a particular era incorporate radio into their beliefs, it does not follow that radio is the sole cause. A chatbot, however, adds a property worth investigating separately: it responds personally and can continue building the narrative.
What We Should Measure to Answer Properly

We need prospective studies with measurements before and after use, information on baseline status, sleep, context, and the products used. We need comparison groups, clinical definitions, and analysis of how people select tools. Someone already vulnerable may seek more conversational support; this direction of the relationship must be separated from the effect of conversation.

It would not be ethical to try deliberately to induce severe episodes to obtain a “clean” experiment. Safety interventions, natural developments, and associations can be studied with appropriate protections. Even then, conclusions must be tied to the product, version, population, and mode of use.

A useful question is whether certain designs reduce the escalation of ungrounded confidence without stigmatizing users or blocking legitimate discussion. Another is: when does an invitation to external verification help, and when is it experienced as abandonment? These are research problems, not arguments for leaving users alone.
Broad Risk May Differ from Severe Clinical Risk

Even if psychosis does not become a universal outcome, other effects may have broader relevance: excessive affirmation, difficulty stopping, postponing decisions, or overestimating productivity. These studies do not tell us how frequent each effect is across all populations. But we can study them without calling them all illnesses.

This distinction changes prevention. We need not assume the whole of society will become psychotic to design systems that are less sycophantic and easier to verify. Nor must we pathologize ordinary use to offer support to those showing serious signs.
The question “will we all?” is dramatic. The better question is: for whom, under what conditions, through what mechanism, and what can we change before the problem worsens?
